extracted.intended_audience: grant writers, nonprofit development staff, and consultants seeking funding
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, tactical guidance for finding grant funding and writing effective nonprofit grant proposals, plus tracking grant-related productivity and demonstrating impact. Targets day-to-day behaviors for staff or consultants responsible for proposal development and funder research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track grant-related productivity and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: At the beginning of your employer’s or client’s fiscal year, create a spreadsheet to track your hands-on time for everything grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track items daily such as staff meetings related to grants; collaborative partner meetings; board meetings preparation and attendance related to grants; grant research time; funder communication and meeting time; grant project planning time; grant writing time; editing and draft feedback time; final grant application package submission time; overtime hours to meet deadlines; grant management and reporting time; grant closeout time; and number of grants you are juggling each year. Use this to document productivity and impact rather than relying on a simple 'win rate' metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight the three Es: education, expertise, and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize your education, expertise, and experience and how you use these to impact organizational and community-wide growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting accomplishments for annual reviews or client reports, explicitly point to the three Es and concrete organizational/community impacts that resulted from your grant work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask associates about corporate vendors and past local funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit down with your work associates and ask who your corporate vendors are, what bank or credit union processes payroll, and what local funders have given money or in-kind contributions in the past five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether you still have good relationships with these funders and whether you can approach them again for support; act on the answers to generate targeted prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visit local banks to find trust officers and hidden funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an appointment to visit every bank in your town, city, village, and county to find out who heads up the trust department (typically a trust officer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust officers manage trust accounts for 'living and dead money‑giving individuals and families' — often not highly advertised sources of grant money. Ask for guidelines on finding and applying to these trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Candid’s Foundation Directory Online at public libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the nearest large public or university library to access Candid’s Foundation Directory Online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a public-access, free-of-charge source for researching foundation and corporate funding sources — a primary research tool for funder identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network with other grantwriters about funding resource subscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Network with other grantwriters to find out about their funding resource subscriptions and what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask peers which subscriptions and resources are effective and consider sharing or subscribing based on peer recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact city and county economic development agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Head down to your city and county economic development agencies to find out about any public monies available for your project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public monies may be available as contracts or grants; economic development offices can point you to local opportunities you might otherwise miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet community foundation staff about capacity building funds
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a community foundation in your county, meet with someone there to ask about the possibility of applying for capacity building funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity building grants can pay for consultants for grant writing, fundraising, board training, and volunteer coordination — useful for strengthening organizational readiness to implement programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call the governor’s office about state agency funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Call your governor’s office and ask about state agency grant funding and other monies that may be available for your organization or business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-level contacts can help you learn about relevant state programs and funding streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend public events and network with local leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend all public events where the 'who’s who' crowd will be gathered and hand out business cards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure your agency’s mission and contact info are on the card and use events to build relationships that may lead to funding or introductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and distribute a press release announcing a funding need
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and distribute a press release to all local and regional media announcing that you have a project in need of funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press coverage can raise visibility and attract potential funders or donors; tailor the release to local/regional outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact your congressional team to track federal funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Call your congressional team members to let them know more about your organization and its need for grant funding, and ask if they can start to track any federal bucks that fit your needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building relationships with congressional staff can help identify federal opportunities and potential referrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use storytelling with supporting statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a storytelling approach (with supporting statistics) in such a compelling way that the reader can’t put down your application until they make a positive funding decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend narrative and data so the proposal is emotionally engaging and credible; make the story concrete and supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a client case study showing real need
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate a case study of a real client your organization has served (change the name for confidentiality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the case study to show a real need of a real person and illustrate how your services address that need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dictionaries and thesauruses to refine vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Take advantage of online dictionaries and thesauruses to expand your command of new words and capture the grant decision maker’s attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful word choice can make your writing more compelling; avoid jargon unless it clarifies meaning for the funder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request FOIA copies of funded government applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to government funding agencies and request (under the Freedom of Information Act) copies of funded grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these funded applications as real examples of award-winning writing and to learn funder expectations and preferred formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and incorporate proven best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Research proven best practices for your proposed solutions and incorporate language from the experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite or align with recognized evidence-based approaches to increase credibility; use expert phrasing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine evaluation results of similar programs
rubrics_metrics.description: When you find best practices, look for the evaluation results of previously implemented programs similar to yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know what works and what doesn’t before you write your proposed solution and cite evaluation findings when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor first-draft creativity (eliminate multiple drafts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate multiple drafts from your writing habits because the most creative and 'wow' words are often the first words you type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider preserving first-draft language rather than over-editing; balance this approach with the need for clarity and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire a proofreader or editor (or get a trusted reviewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hire a proofreader or editor to read your writing and clean it up; if you don’t have money, ask a trustworthy and capable co-worker or friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent review helps catch errors and improve clarity; use external reviewers when possible for objective feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in short, hard-hitting sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in short, hard-hitting sentences — avoid long-winded sentences that almost always lose the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concise, energetic prose that holds reviewer attention; break complex ideas into clear, manageable sentences.
